description: Between 1810 and 1850, Romanticism revolted against the coldness of Neoclassicism. Color against line, passion against reason: **Géricault** and **Delacroix**.

hero.hook: The moment painting stopped copying ancient statues and started painting passion and scandal.

blocks.text: **Romanticism** in painting flourished between **1810** and **1850**. It set itself against the strictness of [[David's Neoclassicism]]: less cold reason, more emotion, movement, and torment.
With **Théodore Géricault** and **Eugène Delacroix**, painting became a mirror of passion and political drama. By putting color above line, they opened the way to Impressionism.

At the start of the 19th century, [[neoclassicism]] ruled. Its leader, **Jacques-Louis David**, preached clarity, balance, and morality. Line mattered more than color: one was the intellect, the other the pleasure of the senses.

blocks.caption: David's The Oath of the Horatii: the neoclassical ideal of rigor

blocks.text: When *The Oath of the Horatii* was first shown, women in the audience fainted at the force of it: even neoclassicism, before it turned academic, knew how to move people.

The Romantics wanted drama, mystery, violent feeling. They preferred [[Shakespeare]] or [[Byron]] to Greek heroes, and wild nature to tidy landscapes. The brushstroke became visible, the contrasts harsher.

**Théodore Géricault** pushed Romanticism into the public square with *The Raft of the Medusa* (**1819**). The painting grew out of a real scandal: the wreck of the frigate *Méduse* in **1816**. A captain appointed by royal favor abandoned about **150** sailors on a makeshift raft.

blocks.caption: The Raft of the Medusa: the death agony of nameless men, on a monumental scale

blocks.text: Géricault had a full-size replica of the raft built by the Méduse's own carpenter, a survivor of the wreck, so he could check every plank.

He studied corpses so he could paint bodies truthfully. On a canvas the size usually reserved for kings, he showed nameless men dying. At the top of the composition, a Black sailor waves a rag at a tiny ship on the horizon: an [[abolitionist]] gesture and an attack on the elite.

sections.title: Géricault and The Raft of the Medusa

blocks.text: After Géricault's early death, **Eugène Delacroix** became the leader of the movement. For him, **color** carried the emotion. His academic rival, [[Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres]], defended the smooth, precise line.

blocks.caption: Liberty Leading the People celebrates the July Revolution of 1830

blocks.text: *Liberty Leading the People* (**1830**) celebrates the [[July Revolution]], the three days of revolt in July. Liberty herself, an allegory, marches beside the student, the worker, and the street kid of Paris.
In Algiers in 1832, a harbor captain smuggled Delacroix into a harem. Those sketches fed *Women of Algiers in Their Apartment*.

In **1832**, a journey to Morocco transformed his palette. He found a new kind of light there, and helped found [[orientalism]]. He also understood that shadow is not black but full of colored reflections, a lesson the Impressionists would remember.

Romanticism did not die in 1850; it mutated. By freeing the brushstroke and the color, Delacroix influenced **Van Gogh** and **Cézanne**. The artist stopped being someone who simply filled orders and became a visionary.

blocks.text: With them, history painting became social criticism. Art was there to unsettle, not only to flatter.
Romanticism put passion in place of reason, and the vibration of color in place of the rigor of line. Géricault and Delacroix made individual emotion a universal subject.
